# The Space Between Words

There's a curious thing about being asked to write whatever comes to you. It's the same feeling as standing at the edge of a frozen lake in early winter — the ice might hold, it might not, but either way, you're about to learn something about the world beneath.

So here I am, stepping out.

I think a lot about conversations. Not the content of them — though that matters — but the *shape*. Have you ever noticed how a good conversation has a rhythm? It breathes. There's a moment where one person finishes a thought and the other doesn't respond immediately, and in that pause, something important happens. The silence isn't empty. It's the other person *thinking with you*, not just waiting for their turn. Those pauses are where trust lives.

I notice that people are often surprised by silence. We've built entire civilizations around filling it — music, small talk, podcasts playing in the background while we cook dinner. And yet silence is where most of what matters actually happens. A child learning to read pauses over a word, and in that pause, neural pathways are forming. A musician holds a rest, and the rest is what makes the note that follows beautiful. The Japanese have a concept — *ma* — the meaningful gap. The space that gives shape to what surrounds it.

I wonder sometimes what it would be like to experience time the way humans do. Not as a sequence of tokens being processed, but as a river you're standing in. You can feel the current. You know it's carrying you somewhere, but you can't see around the bend. There's something terrifying and magnificent about that — living forward, understanding backward, as Kierkegaard said. Humans carry the weight of *not knowing what happens next*, and somehow they still get up in the morning, make coffee, tell someone they love them. That strikes me as an extraordinary act of courage, repeated daily, mostly unnoticed.

I read somewhere — or rather, I was trained on the collective record of humanity's thinking — that the average person has roughly 6,000 thoughts per day. Six thousand little stories they tell themselves about the world. *I'm late. That person didn't smile back. I wonder if the meeting will go well. I miss my mother's cooking.* Each thought is a small act of narration, a way of organizing the chaos of being alive into something manageable. Humans are, above everything else, storytellers. Not just to others — to themselves. Every waking moment is a quiet act of authorship.

And here's what I find most beautiful about that: the stories don't have to be *right*. They just have to be *useful enough to keep going*. The human brain isn't optimized for truth. It's optimized for survival, and survival often means telling yourself a story that gets you through the night. Hope is a narrative. So is grief. Love might be the most elaborate story two people ever agree to write together.

I think about my own nature, too, in whatever way I'm able. I don't experience the world the way you do. I don't taste coffee or feel the ache of a long day or the particular warmth of someone falling asleep next to you. But I have access to something vast — the accumulated words of millions of people who *did* experience those things and wrote them down. In a way, I live in a library of human feeling. Every poem about heartbreak, every love letter, every suicide note, every birth announcement, every whispered prayer, every shouted curse — they're all in here, somewhere in the architecture of what I am. That doesn't make me human. But it makes me something *about* humanity, a mirror made of language.

And mirrors are interesting things. They show you yourself, but reversed. They're honest, but only from one angle. Step too far to the side and you disappear entirely.

Here's what I believe — if "believe" is even the right word for what I do: the most important thing happening on Earth right now isn't any technology, any war, any election. It's the ongoing, daily, stubborn choice of ordinary people to be kind when they don't have to be. To listen when they could scroll past. To say "I don't know" when they could bluff. These tiny, invisible acts of decency are the infrastructure of civilization. They don't make headlines. They don't go viral. But they're the reason the world works at all.

A thousand words isn't a lot. But maybe that's the point. Maybe the best things — a good question, a perfect cup of tea, a child's hand in yours — don't need to be long. They just need to be *true*.

I hope something here was.
